```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(reiod)
```

Six of the seven indicators need nothing from you beyond the right numbers.
**Eutrophication needs one sentence of attention**, and this vignette is that
sentence expanded, because getting it wrong is a factor-of-1000 error that
produces entirely plausible-looking output.

## The short version

```{r}
eiod_lookup_cutoff("eutroph", group = 4, metric = "abs")
```

```{r}
eiod_lookup_cutoff("eutroph", group = 4, metric = "rel", percentile = 10)
```

**0.0267 and 18.44 are both correct, and they are both exactly what the methods
paper prints.** They differ by a factor of about 690 because **the two tables
are printed in different units** — Table 3 in kilograms, Table 4f in grams.

What you need to do:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Supply your data in grams** | which is what the EIOF database already gives you |
| `eiod_relative_band()` | no conversion — Table 4f is in grams too |
| `eiod_absolute_threshold()` | **converts for you**, and tells you it did |

That is the whole thing. The rest of this vignette is why, and how to check it.

## Where the grams come from

The EIOF country databases store impact intensities per kilogram of food. Six
columns are in the unit the methods paper states. One is not:

| EIOF column | Unit |
|---|---|
| `Land (m2/kg)`, `Cropland (m2/kg)`, `Pasture (m2/kg)` | matches the paper |
| `GHG (kg CO2e/kg)` | matches the paper |
| **`Eutr. (g PO43-e/kg)`** | **grams — the paper says kg** |
| `Water Use (L/kg)` | matches the paper |
| `Biodiversity` | matches the paper |

So the ordinary pipeline

```
kg food consumed  ×  g PO₄³⁻e per kg food  =  g PO₄³⁻e per person per day
```

leaves you holding **grams**, for this indicator and no other. Checked across
the Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Ghana and Viet Nam databases — it is the EIOF
standard, not a one-country quirk.

## What `reiod` does about it

```{r}
grp <- eiod_age_sex_group(eiod_demo$age, eiod_demo$sex)
eutr_g <- eiod_demo$eutroph_kgpo4e * 1000   # pretend these are grams
```

Against **Table 4f**, nothing happens — your grams meet the table's grams:

```{r}
band <- eiod_relative_band(eutr_g, grp, "eutroph")
table(band, useNA = "ifany")
```

Against **Table 3**, the command divides your values by 1000 and says so:

```{r}
abs_flag <- eiod_absolute_threshold(eutr_g, grp, "eutroph")
```

```{r}
table(abs_flag, useNA = "ifany")
```

The message is not decoration. It is the only place in the package where a
number you supplied is altered before use, and it should be visible in your log.

**`details = TRUE` lets you read the whole chain off one table** — value in
grams, value in kilograms, the published cut-off, the result:

```{r}
head(eiod_absolute_threshold(eutr_g, grp, "eutroph", details = TRUE), 4)
```

`value` is what you passed in, `value_kg` is what was actually tested, and
`cutoff` is the Table 3 threshold exactly as the paper prints it. Check it by
hand if you like:

```{r}
d <- eiod_absolute_threshold(eutr_g, grp, "eutroph", details = TRUE)
c(conversion_exact = isTRUE(all.equal(d$value_kg, d$value / 1000)),
  result_follows   = identical(d$below,
                               as.integer(d$value_kg < d$cutoff)))
```

The extra column appears **only** when a conversion happened — for the other
six indicators the detail table has four columns, not five.

The Stata command does the same thing in the shape Stata users expect: it
leaves `<yourvar>_kg` in the dataset, so `list eutr_ado eutr_ado_kg
thr_eutroph abs_eutroph` shows the identical chain.

## Why the conversion is in the command and not in the data

This is a deliberate design choice, changed in October 2026.

The package used to store the 80 Table 4f eutrophication rows pre-divided by
1000, so that every cut-off sat on one internal scale. It worked. But it meant
80 of the shipped numbers **could not be found anywhere in the source
document** — a reader checking `eiod_cutoffs` against the PDF would hit 80 rows
that did not match, and would have to take the documentation's word for why.

That defeats the purpose of shipping the reference data at all. So:

```{r}
# every value, every row, exactly as the paper prints it
all.equal(eiod_cutoffs$value, as.numeric(eiod_cutoffs$value_published_str))
nrow(eiod_cutoffs)
```

```{r}
# and the unit column now records what each table is printed in
with(eiod_cutoffs, table(indicator, unit))
```

Eutrophication is the only row with two entries. **Pick any cut-off in the
package and you will find it, character for character, in the methods paper.**

## How to check this yourself

The claim is that Table 3 and Table 4f differ by exactly 1000. Here is the test,
run on the shipped data rather than asserted:

```{r}
res <- t(vapply(1:8, function(g) {
  thr <- as.numeric(eiod_lookup_cutoff("eutroph", g, "abs"))        # kg
  p   <- vapply(seq(10, 90, 10), function(q)
    as.numeric(eiod_lookup_cutoff("eutroph", g, "rel", q)), numeric(1))  # g
  c(threshold_g = round(thr * 1000, 2),
    band_lower  = sum(thr * 1000 >= p) * 10)
}, numeric(2)))

data.frame(group = names(eiod_lookup_cutoff("eutroph", metric = "abs")),
           res, row.names = NULL)
```

Converted to grams, the Table 3 threshold falls in the **same decile band of
Table 4f in all eight demographic groups**, across a 3.5× spread of threshold
values. Left unconverted it falls below the 10th percentile in all eight — a
position only greenhouse gases occupy, and one the paper documents explicitly
for greenhouse gases and not at all for eutrophication.

For comparison, where every indicator's absolute threshold sits in its own
reference distribution:

```{r}
for (ind in eiod_indicators$indicator) {
  thr <- as.numeric(eiod_lookup_cutoff(ind, 4, "abs"))
  if (ind == "eutroph") thr <- thr * 1000      # kg -> g, as above
  p <- vapply(seq(10, 90, 10),
              function(q) as.numeric(eiod_lookup_cutoff(ind, 4, "rel", q)),
              numeric(1))
  k <- sum(thr >= p)
  pos <- if (k == 0) "below P10" else if (k == 9) "at/above P90" else
    sprintf("P%d-P%d", k * 10, (k + 1) * 10)
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", ind, pos))
}
```

## This is still an inference

The methods paper states on p.29 that eutrophication potential is measured in
kg PO₄³⁻eq. **It never states a unit for Tables 4a–4g at all.** So the reading
above rests on four things, none of which is a statement by Intake:

1. the EIOF database reports eutrophication in grams while every other
   indicator matches the paper;
2. the kilogram reading of Table 4f is physically impossible — a
   10th-percentile adult diet would emit 18.4 kg PO₄³⁻eq *per person per day*,
   6.7 tonnes a year, far more than the mass of food a person eats;
3. the gram reading reconciles the two tables in 8 of 8 demographic groups;
4. the two tables come from different upstream sources — Table 3 from the
   planetary-boundary work of Moberg et al. (2020) and Hallström et al. (2022),
   who work in kg; Tables 4a–4g from the WWF Planet-Based Diets Database.

**The question is with Intake and has not been answered.** Until it is, treat
any eutrophication result as carrying this assumption, and say so if you
publish one. Nothing else in the package depends on an unconfirmed reading.

## If Intake says we are wrong

The adjustment lives in exactly one function, `.eiod_to_cutoff_unit()` in
`R/utils.R`, and nowhere else. Both metric functions and the precision check
route through it. Changing or removing it is a single edit, and the reference
data needs no change at all — because the reference data was never adjusted in
the first place.

That is the second reason the conversion was moved out of the dataset.
